narrative:
The model estimated a 64% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it placed your risk at roughly two in three, and because the law school treated that forecast as too high, your application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a judgment that you cannot succeed.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this was the strongest factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the next most influential factor: at 23.50, it was well below the accepted-student average of about 37.18, and it also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. At 2.30 it is below the accepted average of 3.23, but in this prediction it was the only top factor that leaned toward passing; it was not enough to offset the other two.

To improve your position, ask admissions whether you may appeal or receive feedback, and submit any updated evidence: a higher LSAT score, strong recent coursework or academic improvement, and an explanation of circumstances affecting your record. Consider delaying reapplication until you can strengthen these areas, and seek structured bar-exam preparation and academic advising.
